strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observation: the attention-weight analysis (Figs. 2 and 3) convincingly shows that VAR's cross-scale and spatial attention is largely redundant, providing a strong empirical basis for the Markovian assumptions.

Practically significant efficiency gains: elimination of KV cache, ~2.6-3.2x reduction in inference memory, reduced GFLOPs, and the ability to train on 8x RTX 4090 consumer GPUs is a meaningful, reproducible contribution that lowers the compute barrier for next-scale AR models.

The Markovian reformulation does not sacrifice quality: FID improves from 3.55 to 3.09 on ImageNet 256x256 at matched model size (310M), and IS also improves, which is a non-trivial result for an efficiency-oriented method.

Comprehensive ablations: the paper disentangles the contributions of scale-Markov conditioning (Table 3, Fig. 6) and neighborhood size k (Table 4), and reports memory/latency/GFLOPs alongside quality metrics, which supports the design choices (e.g., k=7x7).
Formal complexity analysis (Sections 3.4, Appendix B) clearly substantiates the O(N^2) to O(Nk) claim, and the parallel training strategy with diagonal-pattern causal masks is well described.
Both training-from-scratch (310M) and fine-tuning (600M/1.0B) settings are evaluated, demonstrating generality of the approach.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: spatial-Markov attention is essentially windowed/neighborhood attention directly borrowed from NAT/dilated NAT [13,14], and the scale-Markov conditioning is a natural simplification of VAR's factorization. The contribution is primarily an application of existing attention primitives plus an empirical observation, rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Discrepancies and potential overclaiming in reported speedups: the abstract claims 3.0x average memory reduction, the introduction claims 4.2x (Fig. 2c), and Table 2 shows 2.8-3.2x; these numbers should be reconciled. Additionally, several headline results (Table 2, d20/d24) come from fine-tuning pre-trained VAR checkpoints rather than training from scratch, which complicates attribution of the FID gains to the Markovian design alone.

Evaluation is narrow: only class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 is considered; no higher-resolution, text-to-image, or video experiments, despite the paper motivating high-resolution generation as a key benefit of KV-cache-free inference. Qualitative claims about quality at larger scales remain untested.

Missing quantitative comparison against closely related VAR-efficiency methods (e.g., FastVAR [11], collaborative decoding [4], HART [45]) which target the same memory/latency problems; Table 1 covers only quality-focused baselines, making it hard to judge the competitiveness of MVAR within the efficiency-oriented sub-field.

Some design details weaken the autoregressive framing: for the final two scales (60% of tokens) causal masking is disabled entirely, and ablation results are somewhat noisy (e.g., 3x3 neighborhood outperforms 5x5 in IS; 2 and 3 preceding scales degrade FID while 1 improves it), leaving the precise behavior of the Markov assumption insufficiently explained.
No released code or models at submission time (the 'Codes and models:' field is empty), which limits reproducibility of a paper whose main value lies in practical training recipes.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and empirically supported observation: in VAR, attention concentrates heavily on the immediately preceding scale and on spatially local neighbors, which motivates the scale- and spatial-Markov simplifications.

The efficiency gains are concrete and substantial: elimination of KV cache, ~2.6-4.2x memory reduction, and reduced attention GFLOPs, enabling training on consumer-grade hardware (8x RTX 4090), which is practically valuable for the visual AR community.
The trained-from-scratch 310M model achieves FID 3.09 vs. VAR's 3.55 on ImageNet 256x256, showing the Markovian assumptions do not sacrifice (and slightly improve) generation quality.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated progression from attention-weight analysis (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) to the proposed formulation, and includes complexity analysis, ablations on conditioning prefix length and neighborhood size k, and qualitative results.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: hyperparameters are listed in detail (Table 5) and code/model release is promised.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the scale-Markov assumption essentially amounts to truncating the conditioning prefix to one scale, and the spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/windowed attention, a well-established technique (the paper itself cites neighborhood attention [13,14]). The contribution is primarily an application/engineering combination on top of VAR rather than a new modeling principle.

The comparison for larger models is confounded: MVAR-d20 and MVAR-d24 results come from fine-tuning pretrained VAR checkpoints for 80 epochs, while no baseline fine-tunes the original VAR architecture for the same schedule. Some or all of the FID gains (e.g., 2.95 vs. 2.33) could stem from additional training rather than the Markovian design; a fine-tuned VAR baseline is needed to support the claim that Markovian conditioning itself improves quality.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only class-conditional ImageNet 256x256. No text-to-image, no higher resolutions, and no comparison against other VAR efficiency methods (e.g., FastVAR [11], collaborative decoding [4], HART [45]) despite being cited — the efficiency claims are only benchmarked against vanilla VAR.

Ablations are run only on the 310M model under a short 50-epoch schedule, so conclusions about component contributions (e.g., IS gains of 13.5/13.7) may not transfer to the full models; the main table also shows Recall dropping for MVAR-d16 (0.51 -> 0.48), which is not discussed.

Some inconsistencies reduce confidence: Recall/FID figures for the 310M model differ between Table 1 (3.55/280.4 quoted for VAR) and the ablation baseline (4.84/227.1), the promised code link on page 1 is blank, the duplicate references ([32]/[33], [38]/[39]) and misattributed AdamW citation ([24]) suggest a hasty write-up.

The theoretical complexity claims (O(Nk) vs. O(N^2)) rely on idealized geometric scale growth and hold mainly for attention; the practical speedup reported is modest (1.3-1.7x), suggesting the headline complexity reduction overstates real-world impact.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: the paper provides empirical analysis of attention patterns in VAR (Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 8) to justify two Markovian assumptions (across scales and across space), which grounds the design choices rather than presenting them arbitrarily.

Strong efficiency results: reduction of attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), elimination of KV cache, ~3-4× reduction in inference/training memory, and demonstrated training of a 310M model on eight consumer RTX 4090 GPUs — practically valuable for democratizing VAR-style training.

Solid quantitative results: MVAR achieves FID 3.09 / IS 285.5 at 310M parameters, improving over VAR-d16 (FID 3.55) at equal parameter count and step count, and fine-tuned larger variants (e.g., MVAR-d24† at FID 2.23) are competitive with much larger models.

Reasonable ablation studies covering (i) number of conditioning scales, (ii) neighborhood size k (3×3 to 9×9, selecting 7×7), and (iii) component-wise contributions of scale-Markov vs. spatial-Markov conditioning, with both quality metrics and efficiency metrics reported.
The formal complexity analysis (Section 3.4, Appendix B) is correct in structure and clearly contrasts next-token O(N^3), next-scale O(N^2), and MVAR O(Nk) regimes.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: scale-Markov conditioning is a fairly direct restriction of the conditioning prefix, and spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/dilated-neighborhood attention (cited NAT/NAT-Dilated [13, 14]) applied to the VAR inter-scale attention. The contribution is more an application/recombination of known components than a new modeling principle.

A potential confound in Table 2: the comparison is pre-trained VAR vs. fine-tuned MVAR†, but fine-tuning itself (even under the same architecture) could account for part of the FID/IS gains. A fine-tuned VAR baseline (same epochs, same mask relaxation) is missing to isolate the effect of the Markovian conditioning.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only class-conditional ImageNet 256×256. No text-to-image, no higher-resolution experiments (deferred to future work), and no direct comparison with other efficient VAR variants (e.g., FastVAR [11], Collaborative Decoding [4], HART [45]) despite being cited — these are the most relevant baselines for the efficiency claims.

Inconsistencies in claimed memory reductions: the abstract says 3.0×, the contribution list says 4.2× (inference memory at batch 64), and Table 2 reports 2.8–3.2× at batch 32. These should be stated and scoped consistently.

The Markov assumptions are justified post-hoc using attention maps of a trained VAR, which measures what the trained model does, not the true conditional independence structure of the data; a held-out likelihood or information-flow analysis would strengthen the argument. Additionally, some implementation details (e.g., treatment of within-scale self-attention at scales r9–r10, where causal masking is disabled entirely, and how information flows within a scale) are under-specified.

Mixed quality-metric behavior: Recall consistently drops in MVAR variants (e.g., d16: 0.51→0.48), suggesting a possible diversity reduction that is not discussed. Some ablation claims rest on a short 50-epoch schedule, which may not fully reflect behavior at convergence.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated with empirical analysis: attention-weight studies (Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 15) convincingly demonstrate that in VAR-style next-scale prediction, tokens concentrate on the immediately adjacent scale and on spatially local neighborhoods, which directly motivates the scale-Markov and spatial-Markov assumptions.

The proposed framework yields concrete, measurable efficiency gains: attention complexity reduced from O(N^2) to O(Nk), elimination of the KV cache during inference, ~3x reduction in GPU memory footprint, and faster training/inference, all substantiated in Tables 2, 6, and 7.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: from-scratch training (MVAR-d16, FID 3.09 vs. VAR-d16 3.55 on ImageNet 256x256), fine-tuning of larger models (d20, d24), ImageNet-512, and CelebA/FFHQ experiments, plus component-wise ablations (number of conditioning scales, neighborhood size k, mixed-training ratios in Fig. 9).

The mixed parallel training strategy with diagonal-pattern causal masks is a practical contribution enabling training on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs, and the ablation on training ratios (Appendix D.5) addresses potential concerns about training instability.
The manuscript is clearly written, the formulation (Eqs. 4-7) is sound, and reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameters (Table 5) and a promise of code/checkpoint release.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/local attention (explicitly borrowed from Hassani & Shi 2022/2023), and restricting conditioning to adjacent scales is a first-order Markov simplification of an existing framework (VAR). The contribution is a careful combination of known techniques applied to a new paradigm rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

Fair comparison concerns: the strongest results for large models (d20/d24) come from fine-tuning pretrained VAR checkpoints under a different training schedule (80 epochs, different batch size) rather than matched from-scratch training; some gains could stem from additional optimization rather than the Markovian conditioning. The from-scratch result is limited to the 310M model, and VAR's original schedule (350 epochs, larger batch, different hardware) is not exactly replicated.

Several results are noisy or not fully explained: Table 3 shows non-monotonic quality (2-3 preceding scales degrade FID/IS while 1 improves them), which is counterintuitive and unexplained; no variance or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, so small FID/IS differences (e.g., 3.09 vs. 3.55) have no uncertainty quantification.

The theoretical complexity analysis assumes an idealized geometric scale progression and counts only attention cost; the actual empirical GFLOPs reduction is modest (~1.2x, Table 2), so the O(N^2) to O(Nk) narrative oversells the end-to-end savings.

Scale of evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet (256/512) and small face datasets; there is no text-to-image or very large-scale experiment, so scalability claims beyond ~1-2B parameters remain speculative.

Markovian conditioning risks information loss over long-range structure; while results suggest no degradation, the paper offers limited qualitative or diagnostic analysis of failure cases or of how global coherence is preserved across scales beyond the single ablation.
Some tables contain errors/inconsistencies (e.g., Table 9's FFHQ 9x9 FID(10)=4.99 appears anomalous relative to neighboring values), and recall sometimes decreases in Table 2, which is not discussed.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: empirical analysis of attention weights in VAR (Figs. 2-3) provides concrete evidence that inter-scale and spatial dependencies are redundant, directly motivating the proposed design.

The efficiency gains are substantial and practically relevant: ~3x reduction in inference memory, elimination of the KV cache, and the ability to train on 8x RTX 4090s, with a clean O(Nk) complexity analysis.

Generation quality does not degrade (and slightly improves in FID/IS) despite the restrictive conditioning, which is a non-obvious result; from-scratch training on ImageNet-256 (FID 3.09 vs. VAR's 3.55 at d16) supports this.

Comprehensive ablations: number of conditioning scales, neighborhood size k, mixed training ratios, and additional experiments on ImageNet-512, CelebA, and FFHQ, with detailed hyperparameters supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The two components are straightforward compositions of well-known ideas: conditioning only on the immediately preceding scale is a simple hierarchical factorization, and 'spatial-Markov attention' is essentially neighborhood/windowed attention (Neighborhood Attention, Swin, etc.), which the authors themselves cite. The 'Markovian' framing repackages these known techniques rather than introducing a genuinely new mechanism.

The strongest claim (training from scratch) is only demonstrated for the d16 model. All larger models (d20, d24) are fine-tuned from pre-trained VAR weights, which confounds the comparison: extra fine-tuning epochs alone could improve FID. The claim of 'comparable or superior performance with large fine-tuned models' is thus weaker than presented.

Fine-tuned models show consistent recall drops (0.51->0.48, 0.59->0.56, 0.51->0.48), suggesting the Markovian restriction does lose information, partly contradicting the framing that redundancy is purely wasteful.

Ablations are run at reduced scale (310M, 50 epochs), so the component-level conclusions may not transfer to the full training regime; Table 4 also shows 3x3 achieving higher IS than the chosen 7x7, indicating some instability in the ablation conclusions.

Minor but concerning inconsistencies: the abstract/contributions claim a 3.0x average memory reduction while Fig. 2 and Sec. 3.4 claim 4.2x; Table 9's 9x9 FFHQ row (FID 4.99 at epoch 10) looks anomalous relative to adjacent entries.

The complexity analysis assumes an idealized geometric scale progression that does not match the actual VAR scale sequence {1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,13,16}, so the stated O(Nk) vs. O(N^2) gap is somewhat overstated.
Scope is limited to class-conditional ImageNet-scale generation; no text-to-image or higher-impact applications are demonstrated, which limits significance for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: the paper provides empirical attention-weight analyses (Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 15) demonstrating scale and spatial redundancy in vanilla next-scale prediction (VAR), and then directly converts these observations into two architectural constraints (scale-Markov trajectory and spatial-Markov attention).

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: MVAR-d16 trained from scratch beats VAR-d16 (FID 3.09 vs 3.55), and fine-tuned variants at d20/d24 scale consistently improve FID/IS while reducing inference memory ~3x and eliminating the KV cache entirely, which is a practically significant efficiency win.

The O(Nk) attention complexity analysis (Section 3.4, Appendix A) is correct and cleanly derived, and the claimed complexity reduction is validated by measured GFLOPs and memory numbers rather than only theory.

Extensive ablations: number of preceding scales in the conditioning prefix (Table 3), neighborhood size k across multiple datasets and resolutions (Tables 4, 9), mixed training strategy ratios (Fig. 9), plus additional experiments on ImageNet-512, CelebA, FFHQ, and a 2B model, showing robustness of the design choices.

Notable resource claim: training on eight RTX 4090 GPUs is credible given the memory reductions, and increases reproducibility/accessibility for labs without large A100/H100 clusters. Reproducibility statement and detailed hyperparameters (Table 5) are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/banded attention (Hassani & Shi, 2022; NATTEN), which the authors themselves cite, and the scale-Markov assumption is a direct application of a first-order Markov factorization to VAR. The contribution is more an efficiency-oriented adaptation of known ideas to a recent model than a new modeling principle.

The from-scratch ImageNet comparison is only reported for the d16 configuration; the d20 and d24 results rely on fine-tuning pre-trained VAR weights, and no equally fine-tuned VAR baseline is provided, making it hard to fully disentangle the benefit of the Markovian architecture from fine-tuning and hyperparameter differences (e.g., CFG scale, top-k/top-p differ per model in Table 5).

Precision/Recall trade-offs are somewhat glossed over: in Table 2 fine-tuning slightly reduces Recall at d16 (0.51 to 0.48) and d24 (0.59 to 0.56), suggesting the Markovian restriction may harm diversity/coverage, yet this is not analyzed.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet and small face datasets; no text-to-image or more complex conditional generation, so generalization of the Markovian assumptions to scenarios requiring longer-range global conditioning remains unverified. The authors acknowledge this in limitations but it weakens the significance of the claim that non-adjacent-scale information is truly redundant.

The 'parallel training across scales' claim needs care: training is actually a mixed strategy where scales r9 and r10 (60% of tokens) are still trained separately with custom CUDA kernels; the mixed ratio ablation helps, but the memory/speed numbers depend on this nontrivial engineering and the end-to-end training speedup (1.6-1.7x) is more modest than the memory reduction numbers emphasized in the abstract.

The empirical FID gains over VAR (0.46 at d16 from scratch; ~0.1 at larger fine-tuned scales) are modest relative to the strong framing of 'improving modeling accuracy'; a single-seed result without variance estimates makes these small margins hard to interpret.
